item.title: Before You Call Someone Toxic, Look at Yourself
item.description:
Relationships

Before You Call Someone Toxic, Look at Yourself

Relationships can show us things about ourselves we may not want to see.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Self-reflection can help us recognize our own relationship patterns.
  • A difficult period in a relationship is not toxic, but patterns of disconnection can signal a problem.
  • Relationships can reveal how we communicate, what we tolerate, and what we may need to change in ourselves.
Source: creatifrankenstein/Pixabay

We talk a lot about toxic partners. Toxic relationships.

But what if we are part of the problem? I'm not saying that if someone hurts you, it is your fault. It isn't.

If someone manipulates you, betrays you, or abuses you, that is their responsibility. But relationships are interesting because they show us who we are. How we communicate. What we tolerate. How we react when someone doesn't give us what we want.

When something in a relationship is not right, I ask myself: What am I doing in this relationship?

Because if we never look at our own patterns, we can leave one relationship convinced the other person was the problem, only to recreate the same dynamic somewhere else.

Relationships are messy. People are messy. You will misunderstand each other. You will have days when you don't want to talk. That doesn't mean the relationship is toxic.

But there is a difference between having a difficult moment and developing a pattern that makes the other person feel unsafe, invisible, or emotionally alone.

Sometimes “nothing is wrong” is the problem

Let’s take emotional unavailability as an example. Your partner might come to you and say, “Something is off.” And instead of talking about it, you say, “You're overthinking.” And then you go back to your phone, work, TV show, your life. Done. Problem solved.

Except it isn't. Your partner might want to clear something up that has been bothering them.

And maybe you don't want to hear what comes next. Maybe something has changed. Maybe the relationship has become boring. Maybe you have become distant. Maybe one of you has started thinking about someone else.

And that's why we avoid these conversations. We used to live as we are, in comfort. Why change it?

But eventually, the person stops asking. And then people stop being curious about each other.

My marriage was breaking apart. We didn't enjoy each other's company anymore. We didn't talk on the way to my work or his. We tried to save the marriage many times. We tried dating every weekend, traveling on long weekends, doing workshops. None of it helped because the feelings were gone. No matter how hard you try to love a person, sometimes you cannot make something exist that is no longer there. You can keep convincing yourself otherwise, but eventually that can make your life even more complicated.

article continues after advertisement

For me, staying had started to feel like heavy work. Do I regret leaving? No. Relationship doesn't end because someone leaves. It slowly disappears while both people are still in it.

For some people, dating is the exciting part. You dress up. You go somewhere. You want to impress each other. Then you get married and suddenly your mind switches to: Okay, they're mine now. I can relax. The relationship becomes a routine. Work. Dinner. Netflix. Sleep. Repeat. You no longer ask questions because you think you already know everything about this person.

But do you?

People change. You change. Your partner changes. What they wanted five years ago might not be what they want now. And if you don't keep asking, you might wake up one day next to someone you technically know very well but emotionally don't know at all.

You can know what time they come home and still not know what is happening inside their head.

Isn't that scary?

And then one day, you become interested in someone else. You become curious. You think about them. And immediately, we might think: “I must not love my partner anymore.” Or: “Maybe this new person is my soulmate.” Maybe.

But before you do anything, perhaps ask yourself: Why am I suddenly looking outside my relationship? What's happening inside me? Have I stopped feeling connected? Maybe I have changed. Maybe the relationship has reached a point where we need to have a conversation we have been avoiding for years.

article continues after advertisement

That conversation might save the relationship. Or it might end it. But at least you know what you're dealing with. And sometimes, yes, you need to have the difficult conversation. That is also part of the work.

How much work is too much?

Let's say you are working hard every day to make the relationship better and keep things alive. But how long can you keep working? Nobody can answer that for you. How long is too long? How much effort is enough? When does “working on the relationship” become “I'm forcing something that no longer exists”?

I don't think there is one universal answer. It depends on everyone. Again, go within and ask: What does the work feel like?

Does it feel like you are begging someone to care? Does it feel like you're constantly proving that you deserve basic respect? Then maybe something is wrong.

But if the work makes you curious... If it makes you want to understand your partner better... If you still want to know who they are becoming... If you can have a difficult conversation and somehow feel closer afterward... If the work doesn't feel like punishment but like discovering another layer of the person you love... Then maybe that work is not work in the way we usually think about it.

But maybe you don't want a relationship at all

On the other hand, you might not need any of this. Some people will read this and think: Why do I need another person in my life? Why do I need attachment, arguments, disappointment, compromise? I can live alone. And yes. You can. There is nothing wrong with that.

Some people genuinely love their solo life. They have their own lives, their own routines. And they are happy.

A relationship is not a requirement for a meaningful life.

And there is another group of people. People who don't necessarily want to be alone. They just don't want to be hurt again. They have been betrayed. They have been emotionally abandoned. They gave too much. They trusted someone who didn't deserve their trust. They spent nights crying, trying to understand what happened.

And eventually they say: Never again.

I understand that. After enough pain, being alone can feel like freedom. Nobody can betray you if you don't let anyone close enough to betray you. But if you do want connection, what happens when protecting yourself from pain also protects you from experiencing intimacy and love?

How do we discover our triggers? Our fears?

A relationship can become a mirror. Sometimes you don't like what you see, but that is how life is. Maybe relationships are not here to make us happy but to show us who we are.

Maybe I am emotionally unavailable. Maybe I don't know how to apologize. Maybe I leave too quickly. Maybe I am constantly looking for someone better because I don't know how to tolerate ordinary intimacy. Maybe I blame my partner for everything because it is easier than asking myself what I am contributing. And maybe my partner really is the problem.

article continues after advertisement

Both things can be true. Someone can hurt you, and you can still have something to learn from the relationship.

Only you can decide what to do with what happened to you.

item.title: Zen and the Art of Academia
item.description:
Education

Zen and the Art of Academia

Students, professors, and administrators are on the same path at different times.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Education and learning are processes, not outcomes.
  • Students, professors, and administrators should exist in a flat horizontal hierarchy.
  • We all walk the same path but are just at different time points and physical places.

It's that time of the year again. For some it's back to school. For some it's something they never left. Regardless of point of perspective, training, learning and education are continuous processes. Since 1987 when I started my academic journey as a student at McMaster University in Hamilton until a brain injury ended my career as a professor neuroscience at the University of Victoria, I lived and breathed the academic life as a student, a professor and an administrator. After some reflection I'm sharing some advice for each, with a little help from Bruce Lee, Enter the Dragon and the key reminder that the finger pointing to the moon is not the moon itself.

Students need to know that the core goal of education is to change your mind

Education is a process wherein change is an outcome. Education is not in itself a destination. This is something that is easily confused, especially early on in training. When folks enter training at college or university there is of course a focus on what program and what outcome that is directed towards. This is real and must be acknowledged. But it cannot get in the way of the fact that the outcome is in the future and the training process is now. As students we will, and must, have thoughts for the future but embrace presence in the present.

The student's finger points to the future but goes from a hand in the present. Have a destination in mind but enjoy the experience of the journey.

Professors need to remember that they are guides who previously walked the same path as those they teach

Back in 1675 Sir Isaac Newton, kind of a well known professorial type, wrote that he was "standing on the shoulders of giants". This was an acknowledgement of those who came before him and what he had learned from their exploits, experiences, and greatness. The key thing here is that we all come from somewhere and "somewhen". It's easy to forget that our journey is always an unfolding process that humble us and also keep us grounded in striving to improve.

Professors point to the unfolding path from a place further along the journey but not from above.

Administrators need to know even if you didn't create it, it's your problem to solve

Academic administrators like chairs and deans, take an awful lot of incoming flak, even when it's "friendly fire". Some earn the criticism, but most are just in positions to try and help out but are trying to balance many considerations across many perspectives. A key is to avoid personalizing anything, including your personal responses. Accept things as they are. What is in front of you is in front of you. What you see is what you get. Students study to learn, professors are not above, they are just further along the same path and administrators do not govern, they support. Administrators help maintain the path so that professors can effectively guide and students can find a way to follow.

article continues after advertisement

For administrators, maintaining the integrity of the path means that the finger often points at you. Be authentic in your work, but don't take it personally.

The relationship between training, education, and process

The most famous Samurai in history, Miyamoto Musashi (1584-1645), wrote in Go Rin no Sho that: “The true science of martial arts means practicing them in such a way that they will be useful at any time, and to teach them in such a way that they will be useful in all things.”

I suggest that the "true science of education" can be appreciated in this same way. I think education can begin to approximate the truth that all of life is learning.

My own thinking about academia is heavily influenced by my lifelong study of martial arts. One where ongoing daily training is central, where process is the point, and where a recognition of respect is critical. In this sense training is education and we are all trainees; just at different stages of learning, development, and refining. There's a temptation to put many things, including educational structures, into a vertical hierarchy. Through this lens students (trainees at the earliest stages) are usually at the bottom and professors and administrators jockey for position somewhere up above.

Instead, I strongly prefer a kind of horizontal hierarchy or temporal trail in which everyone has or is walking the same path but are at different points along the timeline. Within this structure it's easier to avoid the trap of separation of categories and more easily appreciate the blending of a continuum of experience.

Every now and then throughout this year and beyond, think about the pointing finger and remind yourself that the finger that points the way is not the way itself. When you find yourself drifting, as we all do, imagine Bruce Lee giving you a mental flick on the forehead to get you back on track. In all aspects of life, it's key to avoid confusing the means for the meaning.
